text: Two delivery services both average 50 minutes per delivery. One is almost always between 48 and 52 minutes. The other ranges from 20 to 80. Same center, completely different experience. A measure of spread tells you how much values vary, and without it a measure of center can be dangerously misleading.
Take two illustrative sets of six delivery times in minutes. Set A: 48, 49, 50, 50, 51, 52. Set B: 20, 35, 50, 50, 65, 80. Both average exactly 50 minutes. Let's see how they actually differ.
The range is maximum minus minimum — 4 minutes for A, 60 minutes for B. It's simple and easy to explain, but it depends only on the two most extreme values, so a single outlier can distort it badly.

The variance asks: on average, how far is each value from the mean, squared? The standard deviation is just the square root of that, which puts the answer back in the original units — minutes, dollars — so it's far easier to interpret. A has a standard deviation of about 1.41 minutes; B has about 21.21 minutes.

Which count you divide by is the most common source of confusion. Population variance divides by n, for when you truly have every value. Sample variance divides by n minus 1, for when your data is a sample estimating a larger population. numpy divides by n unless you pass ddof equals 1; pandas divides by n minus 1 by default — on the values 1, 2, 3, 4, that's 1.25 versus 1.667.

Why n minus 1? A sample's values sit closer to their own mean than to the true population mean, so dividing by n systematically underestimates the spread. Drawing 100,000 samples of 5 values from a distribution with true variance 100: dividing by n lands near 80, too low; dividing by n minus 1 lands right around the true 100. This correction has a name — Bessel's correction.

The interquartile range is the 75th percentile minus the 25th — the spread of the middle half of the data, and like the median, it's robust to outliers. For A that's 1.5; for B it's 22.5. Series.describe prints count, mean, standard deviation, min, the quartiles, and max in one call — usually your first look at any numeric column.

To compare spread across different units, divide the standard deviation by the mean — the coefficient of variation. For A that's about 0.028, for B about 0.424. Choose your measure to match your center: standard deviation with a mean on symmetric data, IQR with a median on skewed data or outliers, and the range for a quick sanity check.
